At the edge of town, where the road forgot to be a road and became two pale tracks through the grass, there was a house with a blue door.

Nobody lived there anymore. Or so everyone said.

In summer, the paint peeled in curls, and the garden grew taller than the windows. In winter, snow gathered on the roof and softened the whole place until it looked less abandoned than asleep. People walked past without looking in. They had errands. They had reasons. They had learned that a shut door was often shut for a reason.

Then, one October evening, a light appeared in the upstairs window.

It was not a bright light. It did not spill down the walls or flash like a signal. It glowed gently, the color of a candle seen through a cup. Still, by morning the whole town knew.

“Probably squatters,” said the grocer.

“Probably a trick of the moon,” said the postmaster, though the moon had been behind clouds.

“Probably nothing,” said everyone else, which is what people say when something has become too interesting to ignore.

Mara went to the house on a Thursday. She was twelve and had recently discovered that adults used the word *probably* when they were afraid of being wrong. She carried a paper bag with two pears in it, because the only thing she knew about visiting mysterious houses was that it seemed rude to arrive empty-handed.

The blue door opened before she knocked.

Behind it stood an old woman in a green cardigan. Her hair was white and braided down her back. She looked neither surprised nor pleased.

“You’re late,” she said.

“I didn’t know I was coming.”

“That’s usually how it happens.”

Mara held out the pears. The woman took one and examined it as if it were a rare jewel. Then she stepped aside.

Inside, the house smelled of dust, cinnamon, and rain. Every wall was covered in clocks. Grandfather clocks, kitchen clocks, little brass clocks no bigger than a coin. Some ticked. Some sighed. Some had stopped at different hours.

“What’s all this?” Mara asked.

“Time,” said the woman.

“I thought time was invisible.”

“So did I, once.”

The old woman led her upstairs, past a narrow window where the evening light lingered. In the room at the top was a small wooden table. On it rested a clock with no hands.

“This one belongs to you,” the woman said.

Mara stared at it. “I don’t want a clock.”

“Good. People who want clocks are always watching them.”

The woman picked up the pear and cut it in half with a silver knife. The two pieces were exactly the same size.

“Time doesn’t only move forward,” she said. “Sometimes it sits beside you. Sometimes it waits. Sometimes it comes back wearing a different face.”

Mara thought of her father, gone two years now, whose laugh she could still hear when the house was quiet enough. She thought of how people said *you’ll get over it*, as though grief were a hill one could simply finish climbing.

The clock without hands gave a small, warm click.

Outside, the clouds parted. Moonlight touched the blue door, and for one second the whole house seemed to shine from within.

Mara stayed until the pears were gone.

When she left, the old woman pressed the other half of the fruit into her hand.

“Will you be here tomorrow?” Mara asked.

The woman smiled. “I’m here whenever you need to be.”

Years later, Mara would forget the exact shape of the house. She would forget the woman’s name, if the woman ever gave one. But she would remember the clock without hands, and the way the old woman had said *wait* as if it were something you could do with courage.

And whenever the world hurried her, whenever every door seemed shut and every answer seemed late, Mara would pause.

She would listen.

Somewhere, she knew, a small clock was still keeping time.
